teach.title: Same endings, a stem that moves

notice.ask: Which word says 'I am' in the first sentence, and 'we are' in the second?

teach.say: A handful of common verbs refuse the ordinary pattern: **the irregular verbs (be, can, go, want, not want, prefer, carry) in the present**. The endings are the familiar *-m* or *-ō*, *-s*, *-t*, *-mus*, *-tis*, *-nt*; the piece in front changes: *su-m*, *es*, *es-t*. *Mārcus in lūdō est* — Marcus is in the school.

teach.title: sum: all six forms
teach.say: *esse* (to be): *sum* I am, *es* you are, *est* he, she or it is; *sumus* we are, *estis* you all are, *sunt* they are. Two stems take turns the whole way through — *su-m*, *es*, *es-t*, *su-mus*, *es-tis*, *su-nt*. The 'I' ending here is *-m*, not the usual *-ō*.

check.ask: Fill the whole present of esse: I am, you are, he is, we are, you all are, they are.

teach.title: possum is pot- with sum on the end
teach.say: *posse* (to be able) is simply *sum* with *pot-* in front, and that *t* becomes *s* whenever *sum* itself starts with *s*: *pos-sum*, *pot-es*, *pot-est*. What follows it is the infinitive (the plain 'to' form): *legere possum*, I can read.

check.ask: possum and potes: which is 'I can' and which 'you can', and what is the stem in each?

teach.title: eō: a verb that is almost only an ending
teach.say: *īre* (to go) has the shortest stem in Latin, *i-*, which stretches to *ī-* in front of most endings: *eō* I go, *īs* you go, *it* he goes, *īmus*, *ītis*, and *eunt* they go. Two to watch: *it* is a whole word, and *eunt* goes back to *e-* rather than *ī-*.

check.ask: īs and eō: who is going in each, and which letters carry the person?

teach.title: volō moves between vol-, vī- and vul-
teach.say: *velle* (to want) changes its stem three times over: *volō* I want, *vīs* you want, *vult* he wants, *volumus* we want, *vultis* you all want, *volunt* they want. *vīs* and *vult* have nothing at all between the stem and the ending, and nothing is missing — that is simply their shape.

check.ask: Fill the two cells where the stem changes shape: 'you want' and 'he wants'.

teach.title: ferō drops the linking vowel
teach.say: *ferre* (to carry) keeps *fer-* the whole way through but drops the linking vowel in front of *s* and *t*: *ferō, fers, fert, ferimus, fertis, ferunt*. So *fers*, *fert* and *fertis* are a syllable shorter than you expect, and *feris* and *ferit* are not Latin at all.

check.ask: Fill the three cells that lost their vowel: 'you carry', 'he carries', 'you all carry'.

core.text: A few very common verbs refuse the ordinary pattern: **the irregular verbs (be, can, go, want, not want, prefer, carry) in the present**. *esse* (be): *sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt*. *posse* (be able): *possum, potes, potest, possumus, potestis, possunt*. *īre* (go): *eō, īs, it, īmus, ītis, eunt*. *velle* (want): *volō, vīs, vult, volumus, vultis, volunt*; *nōlle* (not want): *nōlō, nōn vīs, nōn vult, nōlumus, nōn vultis, nōlunt*; *mālle* (prefer): *mālō, māvīs, māvult, mālumus, māvultis, mālunt*. *ferre* (carry): *ferō, fers, fert, ferimus, fertis, ferunt*. Latin name: verba anomala.
English *be* is irregular the same way: *am, are, is* share no stem, yet they are one verb. Learn these as small tables.
Endings regular; stems change (su- / es-, e- / ī-, vol- / vul- / vī-) or the vowel drops (fers, fert, vult).

invented.en: Marcus does not want to go home.

core.text: The endings are the same six — *sum, es, est* still end in *-m, -s, -t*. What changes is the piece in front: *su-* / *es-*, *e-* / *ī-*, *vol-* / *vul-* / *vī-*. Do not hunt for a conjugation vowel; *fers* and *vult* have none. Read the ending for the person, the stem for the verb.

more.text: *posse* is *pot-* + *esse*, with *pot-* becoming *pos-* before *s*: *pos-sum, pot-es, pot-est, pos-sumus, pot-estis, pos-sunt*. Compounds follow their base verb: *ab-est* (is away), *ad-sunt* (are present), *red-eō* (go back), *ex-it*, *ad-eunt*, *trāns-fert*. *fīō* (become, be made) serves as the passive of *faciō*: *fit, fīunt*. The infinitives are odd too — *esse, posse, īre, velle, nōlle, mālle, ferre* — and the passive infinitive of *ferre* is *ferrī*.

The learner's notes (week 15): a verb counts as irregular if it has more than one stem or breaks the variable-vowel rules; *su / es* uses no variable vowels and takes *-m* for *I*; *possum* is *pos-* + *sum* and *pot-* + *es-*; *e / i* alternates stems and has *eunt*, not *ent*, in the third person plural; *vol / vul / vel / vī* has four stems and uses *-umus*, not *-imus*; *mālō* is *magis* + *volō* and *nōlō* is *nōn* + *volō*, both keeping *-umus*; *fer* has one stem but drops the vowel in *fers, fert, fertis*.

Ørberg (chapter XV) sets *esse*, *īre* and *posse* beside the regular persons (*pos-sumus, pot-estis, pos-sunt*). A&G §199: the old form *volt, voltis* for *vult, vultis* appears in early texts; *nōn vīs* and *nōn vult* never contract.
Learn each as a small table; there is no rule to work them out from. *est* is so ordinary that Latin often leaves a second one out and lets you supply it: *Mārcus in lūdō est, Iūlia in vīllā*.
*nōlle* not to want and *mālle* to prefer are built on *velle* in the same way; the book brings them in later, at chapters XX and XXVIII.
*ferimus* and *ferunt* keep their vowel like any other verb of the third conjugation (the -ere family).
